name: United States v. Nordic Village, Inc.
event: The Sixth Circuit affirmed an order requiring the IRS to pay $20,000 to the bankruptcy trustee.
questions: Whether original Bankruptcy Code §106(c) waives federal sovereign immunity for this monetary recovery, and whether general bankruptcy jurisdiction, an asserted property proceeding or trust principles independently sustain the judgment.
baseline: The three February 25 decisions are uncoordinated and share the law effective through January 27; none uses another February 25 decision as entering law.
record: The United States seeks reversal; the trustee seeks restoration of estate assets through the affirmed money judgment. Nordic Village entered Chapter 11 in March 1984. Officer Josef Lah withdrew corporate money and used $20,000 to pay his individual federal tax liability. The trustee avoided the unauthorized postpetition transfer under §549 and obtained recovery under §550. The judgment is for payment of a sum, not return of an identified fund within the bankruptcy court’s control. Sovereign immunity was raised on appeal; the threshold remains available. No claim-linked waiver under §106(a) or (b) supplies this judgment.
entering: Original §106(c), §549, §550 and then-applicable 28 U.S.C. §1334(d) govern. Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs, 498 U.S. 89; United States v. Mitchell, 445 U.S. 535; United States v. King, 395 U.S. 1; and Ruckelshaus v. Sierra Club, 463 U.S. 680, require unequivocal consent to the monetary remedy. Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance, 492 U.S. 96, has no majority statutory construction controlling the federal sovereign: four votes addressed the text and Scalia’s fifth vote was State-specific. Blatchford v. Native Village of Noatak, 501 U.S. 775, separates jurisdiction from immunity. Whiting Pools, 462 U.S. 198, concerns tangible debtor property; Bull, 295 U.S. 247, and Dalm, 494 U.S. 596, delimit equitable recoupment. Simulated Ardestani (December 10) controls actual INA/APA fee coverage, not a new residual-waiver rule. Wolas and Dewsnup address different Code provisions and do not decide §106.
reach: Federal sovereign consent is resolved before enforcement of the recovery remedy. The interpretation is a legal question, not a heightened proof burden for the transfer. State immunity, a genuine specific-property case and any later amendment are not reached.
stoneCheck: The original statutory language, monetary judgment and independent entering waiver authorities fit the approved core. Stone joins only the Court’s limited monetary-waiver construction and its actual-judgment alternatives. No proposition barring every true in rem proceeding or validating the diversion is adopted.
action: The Sixth Circuit’s judgment is reversed, 7–2. The personal monetary judgment against the United States cannot stand without the required sovereign consent.

holdings.title: Original §106(c) does not clearly authorize this monetary recovery
holdings.rule: Original Bankruptcy Code §106(c) does not unequivocally waive the United States’ immunity from an affirmative personal money judgment recovering an unauthorized transfer under §550. A plausible construction giving the clause binding nonmonetary or claim-determination effect defeats the required clear consent to this monetary remedy; §106(a) and (b) retain their express claim and offset operations.
holdings.authority: Scalia’s opinion, joined by Stone, White, O’Connor, Kennedy, Souter and Thomas; seven of nine Justices control the statutory threshold.
holdings.explanation: The Court holds that applying bankruptcy provisions to government does not by itself authorize every monetary remedy against the Treasury. Irwin requires unequivocal statutory consent, while Hoffman supplies persuasive statutory analysis without a majority holding binding this federal case. Subsections 106(a) and (b) expressly address claims and offsets; subsection (c) instead makes designated provisions applicable and determinations binding. Reading its paragraphs together allows meaningful determinations of governmental rights and estate liabilities without an affirmative payment order. Its introductory exception also permits a reading preserving the neighboring limits on monetary claims. The trustee’s broader construction is plausible, but that does not make it unequivocal. Legislative history cannot supply the clear statutory expression missing from the enacted provision. Section 550 establishes ordinary recovery authority but does not answer the separate sovereign-consent question. The decision does not approve Lah’s diversion, render subsection (c) ineffective, resolve state constitutional immunity, or determine the operation of a different waiver.
precedents: *Irwin v. Department of Veterans Affairs*, 498 U.S. 89 — applied: the particular monetary remedy requires unequivocal statutory consent.
*United States v. Mitchell*, 445 U.S. 535 — applied for the same express-consent requirement.
*United States v. King*, 395 U.S. 1 — applied for the same express-consent requirement.

*Hoffman v. Connecticut Department of Income Maintenance*, 492 U.S. 96 — its plurality’s statutory reasoning is adopted for this federal issue; its fractured state judgment is not treated as controlling federal-waiver precedent.
*Ruckelshaus v. Sierra Club*, 463 U.S. 680 — applied: consent is not enlarged beyond what Congress’s language requires.
*McMahon v. United States*, 342 U.S. 25 — applied: consent is not enlarged beyond what Congress’s language requires.
*United States v. Menasche*, 348 U.S. 528 — applied to preserve operative work for both paragraphs of §106(c).
*Dellmuth v. Muth*, 491 U.S. 223 — its textual clear-statement reasoning supports requiring clarity in enacted language; no new decision about States is made.

holdings.title: Jurisdictional and property labels do not sustain this money judgment
holdings.rule: A general grant of jurisdiction over bankruptcy-estate property in §1334(d), an asserted trust interest, or the origin of transferred money in estate assets does not supply federal consent to this personal money judgment. Because the trustee seeks a sum rather than identified property under the court’s control, this order cannot be sustained as a genuine property adjudication or as equitable recoupment.
holdings.authority: Scalia’s opinion, joined by the same seven Justices, resolves each alternative ground necessary to the threshold disposition.
holdings.explanation: The Court also holds that the judgment cannot be preserved by changing its label. Blatchford distinguishes a court’s jurisdiction over a class of claims from the sovereign’s amenability to the requested relief. Section 1334(d) provides the former and does not conceal the latter. The trustee obtained a general obligation to pay $20,000; no identified property supports the asserted proceeding against a particular fund. Whiting Pools required return of tangible debtor property seized before bankruptcy and did not establish consent to payment of money from the Treasury. Begier’s attention to particular property does not turn the historical source of these funds into a presently identified fund. Nor do trust principles governing private owners enact sovereign consent. Bull concerns equitable recoupment, whose limited operation Dalm preserves; this affirmative recovery is not that defense. Genuinely distinct specific-property remedies require their own facts and authority and are not adjudicated on an invented record here.
precedents: *Blatchford v. Native Village of Noatak*, 501 U.S. 775 — applied for the distinction between jurisdiction and immunity.
*United States v. Whiting Pools, Inc.*, 462 U.S. 198 — distinguished: tangible debtor-property turnover does not authorize this Treasury payment.
*Begier v. IRS*, 496 U.S. 53 — distinguished: no identified fund supports the actual order.
*United States v. Shaw*, 309 U.S. 495 — preserved as contrary to inferring monetary consent from a property characterization.
*Bull v. United States*, 295 U.S. 247 — equitable recoupment retains its limited defensive operation; it does not sustain this affirmative award.
*United States v. Dalm*, 494 U.S. 596 — equitable recoupment retains its limited defensive operation; it does not sustain this affirmative award.

law: Effective February 25, original §106(c) supplies no waiver for the personal money recovery at issue. The rule before the event required unequivocal consent but left this federal application of Hoffman’s fractured analysis unresolved; the rule afterward resolves that application and rejects the specific alternative routes. Claim-linked waivers, actual property remedies and the underlying avoidance provisions retain their own requirements. No constitutional immunity rule for States or later statutory waiver is decided.
separate: Stevens, joined by Blackmun, reads the notwithstanding-immunity clause, the covered term in §550 and the binding-determination language as authorizing recovery. They regard the narrower constructions as inconsistent with the enacted text and supported bankruptcy purpose, and would affirm the award. Their criticism of restrictive sovereign-immunity rules does not change the Court’s rule.
continuity: Stevens and Blackmun, dissent, February 25: §106(c)’s express application-and-binding language reaches §550 monetary recovery; sovereign-immunity construction should not defeat that legislative command. They also criticize rigid judge-made immunity presumptions. Noncontrolling; no later treatment.
procedure: Supreme Court review ends with reversal. The $20,000 personal judgment is set aside. Ordinary proceedings may address a genuinely distinct and properly supported remedy, but no substitute relief, fund identification or further Supreme Court event is ordered.
dependencies: Holywell shares the predecision baseline and does not derive its tax obligations from this ruling. Later bankruptcy money claims must identify the applicable waiver and actual remedy.
formBasis: 7–2 judgment; the non-Stone votes, controlling monetary-waiver and alternative-ground coalitions, remedy and precedent treatment match the comparator apart from Stone’s replacement of Rehnquist. Reservations concerning a different genuine property case do not decide that reserved issue.
sourceMap: 503 U.S. 31–32 verifies the transfer, courts below and original §106 text; pages 33–37 verify Hoffman’s topology and waiver alternatives; pages 37–39 verify the actual remedy and alternative grounds; pages 39–46 verify the dissent.

alternatives: The trustee’s text-plus-§550 path has substantial textual support but not the unequivocal consent the seven-Justice coalition requires. The narrower construction gives §106(c) independent work without erasing (a)/(b). The general-jurisdiction route confuses forum power and waiver; the property route lacks an identified res; the trust/recoupment route does not describe the relief entered. Hoffman’s state-specific fifth vote cannot be counted as a federal statutory majority.
auditFinal: Final judgment and both controlling grounds have seven votes. Stevens/Blackmun retain their competing statutory interpretation. The historical Ardestani residual-canon citation is not imported: independent surviving authorities supply the canon, while simulated Ardestani remains its source-specific coverage holding. This does not alter a non-Stone result or level of generality.
